The second-generation A1 arrived in 2018 on the MQB A0 platform, transitioning fully to EA211 1.0 and 1.5 TSI engines, with a 2.0 TSI EA888 added for the 40 TFSI variant in 2019. Both generations share the EA211 family across their later model years, making it the dominant petrol architecture for the A1 nameplate.

items.text: The late D2 (2000-2002) carried over Audi's pre-millennium V6/V8 petrol architecture (30-valve V6, 40-valve V8) alongside the first W12 application in a production Audi.

The D3 (2002-2009) introduced FSI direct injection across the petrol range (2.8, 3.2, 4.2) and the 3.0 TDI V6 that would become the A8's volume diesel for two decades. The S8 D3 used the Lamborghini-derived 5.2 V10 FSI, while the 4.2 TDI V8 offered the highest torque output of any A8 diesel at that point.
The D4 (2010-2017) consolidated around the EA837 3.0 TFSI supercharged V6 and the 3.0 TDI V6 as core powertrains, with the S8 adopting the 4.0 TFSI twin-turbo V8 from 2012.
The current D5 (2017-present) introduced 48V mild-hybrid technology across the 50 TDI and 55 TFSI, and the 60 TFSI e PHEV paired the 3.0 TFSI with an electric motor.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Audi A8?
items.a: The Audi A8 has used four core engine families since 2000: the EA837 3.0 TFSI V6 (petrol, D4–D5), the 3.0 TDI V6 (diesel, D3–D5), the 4.0 TFSI V8 (S8, D4–D5), and the 4.2 FSI V8 (petrol, D3–D4). Conditional/low-volume families include the W12, 4.2 TDI V8, and 5.2 V10 (S8 D3). Check the generation and variant tables above for the exact engine fitted to your car.

items.q: How do I identify which engine my Audi A8 has?
items.a: Use the vehicle registration checker to confirm the model year and badge, then check the V5C logbook's "engine code" field (Section 4, field P.5). Common A8 codes include CGWD/CREA (3.0 TFSI), CDTC/CTBA/DDVC (3.0 TDI), CEUA/CTGA/CWGA (4.0 TFSI S8), and BVJ/CDRA (4.2 FSI). Always confirm the engine code matches your generation before ordering.

For the 4.0 TFSI V8 (S8), reconditioned is strongly recommended due to the engine's complexity and high replacement cost.

items.text: The Citroën C4 launched in 2004 on the PF2 platform, replacing the Xsara. Mk1 engines included TU-series petrols (1.4i, 1.6i), the 2.0i (EW10J4), the 1.6 THP (EP6DTS) turbo petrol, and a 1.6 VTS high-output version.

Diesel options included DV6 (HDi and BlueHDi, 92–120PS) and DW10 (150PS). The Mk3 (2018) moved to a crossover/SUV body on the EMP2 platform, adopting PureTech EB2 (100–155PS) and DV5 (1.5 BlueHDi, 100–130PS) diesels, with DW10 (150PS) in higher trims.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Citroën C4?
items.a: The C4 had four engine families across three generations. Mk1 (2004–2010) had TU-series, 2.0i, EP6/Prince, DV6, and DW10. Mk2 (2010–2018) had PureTech EB2, EP6/Prince, DV6, and DW10. Mk3 (2018–present) has PureTech EB2, DV5, and DW10.

items.q: How do I identify which engine is in my C4?

generations.title: C3 Aircross Engines Through the Generations

items.text: The C3 Aircross launched in 2017 as Citroën's compact crossover, positioned below the C5 Aircross. The engine range was drawn entirely from PSA's shared architecture: the PureTech 1.2-litre three-cylinder turbo petrol (EB2 family) in 82, 110, and 130 PS outputs, and the DV6 1.6-litre four-cylinder diesel in 1.5-litre (DV5RD, 102–120 PS) and 1.6-litre (DV6FD, 99 PS) variants. The 1.5 BlueHDi gradually replaced the 1.6 BlueHDi from around 2018. The PureTech petrol engines became the dominant UK choice, with the 110 PS version being the best-selling variant. The second-generation C3 Aircross launched in 2025 with a rationalised engine range — diesel was dropped entirely. The range consists solely of 1.2-litre PureTech petrol engines: a 98–100 PS turbo non-hybrid, a 136 PS mild-hybrid, and a 145 PS mild-hybrid. The mild-hybrid system pairs the 1.2-litre three-cylinder engine with a 48V battery and six-speed dual-clutch automatic gearbox, reflecting broader UK market trends away from diesel.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Citroën C3 Aircross?
items.a: The C3 Aircross was offered with 2 engine families across its production run. Petrol engines are all from the PureTech (EB2) family: a 1.2-litre three-cylinder turbo in 82, 100, 110, 130, 136, and 145 PS outputs. Diesel engines are from the DV6 family: a 1.5-litre BlueHDi (DV5RD, 102–120 PS) and a 1.6-litre BlueHDi (DV6FD, 99 PS). The 2025–present second generation is petrol-only, with 1.2 Turbo and 1.2 Hybrid variants.

items.q: How do I identify which engine my C3 Aircross has?
items.a: Check your V5C registration document — the engine code is listed in Section 4 (Vehicle details). Common codes for the C3 Aircross include EB2FA (1.2 PureTech 82), EB2DT/EB2ADT (1.2 PureTech 110), EB2ADTS (1.2 PureTech 130), DV5RD (1.5 BlueHDi), and BHY/DV6FD (1.6 BlueHDi). For older vehicles, confirm the production year — the 1.2 PureTech 82 was phased out around 2020, and the 1.6 BlueHDi was available alongside the 1.5 BlueHDi in early production years. You can also use an online reg-checker service (e.g., the DVLA vehicle enquiry service) which will show your vehicle's engine details.

items.q: Should I buy a used or reconditioned C3 Aircross engine?
items.a: For the PureTech 1.2 petrol (EB2), used engines with low mileage are often the most cost-effective option, but be aware of known timing belt degradation issues — the belt runs in oil and can shed material, blocking the oil pickup. A reconditioned engine with a new timing belt, oil pump, and pickup strainer offers better long-term reliability than a high-mileage used unit. For the 1.5 BlueHDi diesel (DV5RD), high-mileage examples may benefit from a reconditioned unit with new injectors, EGR cooler, and timing components.

items.text: The Juke launched in 2010 as Nissan's quirky compact crossover, offered with a choice of two petrol engines — the 1.6 naturally aspirated HR16DE and the 1.6 DIG-T turbocharged MR16DDT — plus a Renault-sourced 1.5 dCi diesel K9K. The turbocharged petrol became the core Juke engine, offering strong performance for the segment. The Nismo variant arrived in 2013, using a higher-output version of the MR16DDT. The second-generation Juke went on sale in 2019 on Nissan's CMF-B platform, with the HR16DE dropped in favour of the Renault-sourced 1.0-litre three-cylinder turbo H5Bt, while the MR16DDT continued. No diesel was offered in the F16 generation, reflecting the declining UK diesel market.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Nissan Juke?
items.a: The Juke was offered with four engine families across its production run. Petrol engines include the 1.6 HR16DE naturally aspirated (2010–2019), the 1.6 MR16DDT turbocharged (2010–present, including Nismo variants), and the Renault-sourced 1.0 H5Bt turbo (2019–present). Diesel engines include the Renault-sourced 1.5 K9K dCi (2010–2019). All engine families are available through Engined's direct-purchase platform with fixed prices and warranty.

items.q: How do I identify which engine my Juke has?
items.a: Check your V5C registration document — the engine code is listed in Section 4. For F15 Juke models (2010–2019), common codes include HR16DE (1.6 petrol), MR16DDT (1.6 turbo petrol), and K9K (1.5 diesel). For F16 Juke models (2019–present), look for H5Bt (1.0 turbo petrol) or MR16DDT (1.6 turbo petrol). You can also use an online reg-checker service which will show your vehicle's engine details.

items.q: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Juke engine?
items.a: This depends on your budget and the age of your vehicle. For newer F16 models, used engines with low mileage are often the most cost-effective option. For the MR16DDT 1.6 DIG-T turbo, early examples can suffer from timing chain stretch and carbon build-up — a reconditioned engine with new timing components may be a better long-term investment. The K9K diesel is generally robust but high-mileage examples may benefit from a reconditioned unit with new injectors and turbo components. The HR16DE is a simple, reliable unit — used examples with moderate mileage are a safe choice.

items.q: What is your warranty and delivery standard?
items.a: All GMC engines come with a standard warranty covering mechanical failure. Delivery is to a UK mainland address of your choice. Used engines are photographed and compression-tested before dispatch; reconditioned engines are fully rebuilt with new gaskets, seals, timing components, and bearings. Detailed warranty terms are available on each listing page.

The 1.2 TCe (H5F) joined the range at the 2012 facelift. Diesel options expanded to include the 1.6 dCi (R9M) from 2012, while the Renault Sport variant evolved through 250, 265, and 275 PS outputs using the F4R 874 engine.

The fourth-generation Mégane (2015–2023) launched with 1.2 TCe (H5F) petrol and 1.5 dCi (K9K) and 1.6 dCi (R9M) diesels. The 1.3 TCe (H5H) replaced the 1.2 in 2018; the 1.8 TCe RS (M5P) arrived in 2017 in 280 and later 300 PS forms. A 1.0 TCe (H5D) joined at the 2020 facelift, and a 1.6-litre plug-in hybrid (H4M-based E-Tech) was introduced in 2020.

items.q: Which engines are fitted to the Renault Megane?
items.a: The Renault Megane uses three core engine families: K9K 1.5 dCi, R9M 1.6 dCi, and the Energy TCe family of turbo petrols (including H5F 1.2, H5H 1.3, H5D 1.0, and M5P 1.8 RS). A conditional legacy petrol (K4M 1.6) covers older models where trade evidence exists.

items.q: How can I identify which engine is in my Megane?
items.a: Check the V5C registration document for the engine number; the engine code is also stamped on the engine block plate. For Megane IV, the engine type is listed on the engine plate with codes including H5F Turbo, H5H Turbo, H4M, M5P Turbo, K9K, R9M, and R9N.

items.q: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Megane engine?
items.a: For Megane's K9K and R9M diesel families, used engines are widely available and represent the most cost-effective option for older cars. For Energy TCe petrol turbos (particularly 1.2 TCe), verify timing chain condition — reconditioned units may offer better longevity for high-mileage cars.

items.text: The first-generation Scenic (2000–2003) launched with 1.4 and 1.6 petrol units (K4J/K4M) and the 1.9 dCi diesel (F9Q) – Renault’s early common-rail offering – plus a 2.0 16v (F4R) flagship. These engines were carried over from the Mégane I platform.

The second generation (2003–2009) introduced the 1.5 dCi (K9K) as the main diesel alongside the 1.9 dCi, while the 1.6 16v petrol continued; a post-facelift (2006) added a 2.0 dCi (M9R) for higher-power diesel demand, and the 2.0 petrol was phased out.

The third generation (2009–2016) saw the arrival of the 1.6 dCi (R9M) replacing the 1.9 dCi, and the first turbo petrol – the 1.2 TCe (Energy TCe) – introduced at the 2012 facelift; the 1.5 dCi remained the volume diesel.

The latest fourth generation (2016–present) continues with the 1.5 dCi, 1.6 dCi, and Energy TCe petrols; a 1.3 TCe replaced the 1.2 after the 2019 facelift. No full-electric version is sold under the Scenic nameplate.

items.q: What engines are fitted to the Renault Scenic?
items.a: Renault Scenic generations have used 1.4/1.6 petrol (K4J/K4M), 1.9/2.0 diesel (F9Q/M9R), and later 1.5/1.6 dCi (K9K/R9M) plus 1.2/1.3 TCe petrol. The current range covers three core engine families across four generations.

items.text: The SEAT Arona arrived in 2017 as a subcompact crossover built on the MQB A0 platform, sharing its underpinnings with the Ibiza. Right from launch, the Arona relied exclusively on the EA211 petrol engine family – no diesel or hybrid options were ever offered in the UK. The initial range comprised two 1.0-litre TSI tunes: 95 PS for entry-level SE and SE Technology trims, and 115 PS for FR and XCellence models. In 2018, SEAT expanded the line-up with a 1.5-litre TSI evo producing 150 PS, reserved for higher-spec FR and XCellence cars. The 2020 facelift brought a standardisation of the 1.0 TSI to 115 PS across most trims, while the 95 PS version remained on the most affordable SE models. Throughout its production, the Arona has never been sold with a diesel engine in the UK, despite the EA189 and EA288 units being common elsewhere in SEAT’s range. This single-engine-family approach makes replacement straightforward: every Arona engine is an EA211 variant, differing only in tuning and displacement. Today, the Arona continues with the same powertrain philosophy, offering buyers a simple, reliable choice of petrol engines across all trims.

items.q: What engines are fitted to the SEAT Arona?
items.a: The SEAT Arona is powered exclusively by the EA211 family of petrol engines: 1.0 TSI 95 PS, 1.0 TSI 115 PS, and 1.5 TSI 150 PS. options.title: Used S-Cross engines
options.text: Used engines are the most common choice for the S-Cross's D13A diesel — this Fiat-sourced Multijet unit was widely fitted and used examples are plentiful and cost-effective. For the 1.6 petrol M16A (fitted to early models), used engines are typically sufficient and represent the most affordable route to getting the car back on the road. All used engines are inspected and tested before listing.

options.title: Reconditioned S-Cross engines
options.text: For S-Cross's Boosterjet engines, coolant hose issues are a known concern on early units — reconditioned units may offer better reliability with updated components and full machining work. Reconditioned engines come with a more comprehensive warranty and are fully rebuilt to factory tolerances, making them the preferred choice for owners planning to keep the car long-term.

items.text: The S-Cross launched in 2013 as the successor to the SX4, powered by a 1.6-litre VVT petrol (M16A, 120 PS) and a 1.6-litre DDiS diesel (D16AA, 120 PS) — both naturally aspirated four-cylinder units carried over from the SX4.

The 2017 facelift introduced the Boosterjet turbo family: a 1.4-litre (K14C, 140 PS) and a 1.0-litre three-cylinder (K10C, 111 PS), while the 1.6 petrol and 1.6 DDiS diesel were dropped in 2019. That same year, the 1.3 DDiS diesel (D13A, 95 PS) — a Fiat-sourced Multijet — replaced the 1.6 DDiS.
The current S-Cross continues with Boosterjet turbos (1.4 and 1.0) plus a mild-hybrid 1.4 variant (129 PS), while an entry-level 1.5 naturally aspirated petrol (K15B) is offered in some markets.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Suzuki S-Cross?
items.a: The S-Cross was offered with three core engine families: Boosterjet turbo petrols (1.0 and 1.4), a K-series larger 1.5 naturally aspirated petrol, and the D13A 1.3 diesel (Fiat-sourced Multijet). Early generations also used a 1.6 petrol (M16A) and a 1.6 diesel (D16AA), with the diesel now confirmed missing from the current registry. The three core families cover all generations from 2013 to the present.

items.q: How do I identify which engine is in my S-Cross?
items.a: Check your V5C registration document for the engine number or look for the engine code stamped on the block plate. Common S-Cross engine codes are K14C (1.4 Boosterjet), K10C (1.0 Boosterjet), K15B (1.5 K-series), D13A (1.3 diesel), M16A (1.6 petrol), and D16AA (1.6 diesel). If you're unsure between early and late models, use our registration checker to confirm fitment — especially for the 2019 changeover when the 1.3 diesel replaced the 1.6.

items.q: Should I buy a used or reconditioned engine for my S-Cross?
items.a: For S-Cross's Boosterjet engines, coolant hose issues are a known concern on early units — reconditioned units may offer better reliability. For the D13A diesel (Fiat-sourced), used engines are widely available and cost-effective. For the 1.6 petrol (M16A), used engines are typically sufficient. Choose based on your budget and how long you plan to keep the vehicle.

options.title: Used Swift engines
options.text: A used Swift engine is the most cost-effective route for most buyers, particularly for the earlier K-series and M-series petrols that are plentiful in UK breakers. Used units typically come from low-mileage accident-damaged cars and can be fitted immediately. For the common 1.2 and 1.0 engines, a used unit offers excellent value and immediate availability.

options.title: Reconditioned Swift engines
options.text: Reconditioning is the recommended route for higher-mileage Swift engines, especially the turbocharged Boosterjet units where wear on the turbocharger and cooling system can be an issue. A reconditioned engine is stripped, inspected, and rebuilt to factory tolerances with new bearings, rings, and gaskets. This option makes particular sense for the Sport 1.4 Boosterjet, where the engine has been driven hard.

items.text: The Swift launched in 2005 with a range of K-series and M-series petrols (1.0, 1.2, 1.3, 1.5) alongside a Fiat-sourced 1.3 DDiS diesel (D13A), and the Swift Sport arrived with a 1.6 M16A producing 125PS.
The fourth-generation Swift (2010) continued with K-series and M-series petrols, introduced the Dualjet 1.2, and retained the D13A diesel, while the Sport's 1.6 was updated to 136PS.
The fifth-generation (2017) brought Boosterjet turbo petrols (1.0 K10C, 1.4 K14C) and the K12C SHVS mild-hybrid, with the Sport switching to a 1.4 Boosterjet in 140PS (later detuned to 129PS).
The current Swift continues with the 1.2 SHVS mild-hybrid and 1.4 Boosterjet Sport, with reduced outputs for emissions compliance.

items.q: What engines are fitted to the Suzuki Swift?
items.a: The Suzuki Swift has used five engine families: K-series small petrols (K10B, K12B), the Fiat-sourced D13A diesel, Boosterjet turbos (K10C, K14C), Dualjet 1.2, and K12C SHVS mild-hybrid. Earlier Mk3 and Mk4 cars also used M-series petrols (M13A, M15A, M16A). Today's Swift uses 1.2 SHVS and 1.4 Boosterjet units.

items.q: How do I identify my Swift's engine?
items.a: Check your V5C logbook for the engine code, or use an online registration checker for a quick identification. For transition-year cars (particularly 2010 and 2017 facelifts), the engine code on the block itself is the definitive identifier — K10B/K12B are 1.0/1.2 non-turbo, K10C/K14C are Boosterjet turbos, and K12C is the mild-hybrid.

items.q: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Swift engine?
items.a: For the Swift, K-series and Boosterjet engines are common; reconditioned units are recommended for higher-mileage cars. The D13A diesel has good parts availability. A used unit is fine for lower-mileage petrols, but the turbocharged Boosterjet benefits from a reconditioned unit given its higher-stressed components.

items.q: What warranty and delivery do you offer?
items.a: Every Swift engine we sell comes with a comprehensive warranty that covers parts and labour against manufacturing defects. We deliver across the UK with fully tracked shipping, and our fitment guarantee ensures you get the right engine for your specific registration and chassis code.

items.text: The first-generation Grand Vitara (FT/GT, 1998–2005) offered Suzuki's G-series and J-series petrols (1.6 G16B, 2.0 J20A), alongside a 2.0-litre diesel and the Renault-sourced 1.9 DDiS.
The second-generation Grand Vitara (JT, 2005–2015) introduced the 1.6 VVT (M16A) as the entry petrol, with the 2.0 VVT (J20A) and later 2.4 VVT (J24B) as higher-output options.

The third-generation Vitara (LY, 2015–present) dropped diesel entirely, adopting Suzuki's Boosterjet turbo petrol family (1.4 K14C 140PS, 1.0 K10C 111PS) and the 1.6 VVT (M16A) as the naturally-aspirated option.

items.q: 1. What engines were fitted to the Suzuki Vitara/Grand Vitara?
items.a: The Vitara has used five main engine families across its three generations. Petrol: legacy 1.6/2.0/2.4 NA petrols (G16B, J20A, J24B, M16A), K-series larger (K14B/K15B), and Boosterjet turbo (K14C, K10C, K14D). Diesel: 2.0 TD, 1.9 DDiS (Renault-sourced, 100–129PS), and D13A (Fiat Multijet, 95PS). The third generation (2015–present) is petrol-only.

items.q: 2. How can I identify my Vitara's engine?
items.a: Use a free online vehicle registration checker (e.g., DVLA vehicle enquiry, Parkers) to confirm the engine code. The V5C logbook shows the engine number and capacity. The engine code is stamped on the front of the engine block, near the timing cover. For first-generation cars, codes begin with "G" (G16B), "J" (J20A), or "F" (F9Q for 1.9 DDiS). For second-generation cars, codes include "M16A", "J24B", and "D13A". For third-generation cars, codes begin with "K" (K14C, K10C, K14D).

items.q: 3. Should I buy a used or reconditioned Vitara engine?
items.a: For Boosterjet turbo petrols, used engines are widely available and generally reliable — the 1.4 Boosterjet has proven robust in UK market. For D13A (Fiat Multijet) diesels, used units are the default choice — these engines are well-proven and widely available. For legacy petrols (G16B, J20A, J24B, M16A), used units are available but ageing; reconditioned units may be preferable for higher-mileage examples. The 1.9 DDiS is a Renault-sourced engine — used units are available, but check for turbo and injector wear.

items.q: 4. What warranty and delivery do you offer?
items.a: All GMC engines are sold with a 12-month parts-only warranty as standard, with an upgrade path to a 24-month fitted warranty through approved partner garages. Delivery is UK-wide via palletised courier with 48-hour dispatch on stocked units.

items.text: The Auris launched in 2007 as Toyota's new C-segment hatchback, replacing the Corolla in Europe. Built at Toyota's Burnaston plant in Derbyshire, the Mk1 launched with 1.4 and 1.6-litre petrol units and 1.4, 2.0 and 2.2-litre D-4D diesels. In 2009, the 1.33 Dual VVT-i (1NR-FE) replaced the 1.4 VVT-i, and a refreshed styling was introduced in 2010. The Auris Hybrid, Toyota's second hybrid model after the Prius, launched in 2010 using the same 1.8-litre petrol-electric running gear as the third-generation Prius.

The second-generation Auris launched in 2012 with a choice of 1.33 or 1.6-litre petrol engines, a 1.4-litre diesel, and the 1.8-litre Hybrid. The Touring Sports estate joined the range in 2013. A major 2015 facelift brought new powertrains: the 1.2-litre turbo petrol (8NR-FTS) replaced the 1.6 Valvematic, and the 1.6-litre D-4D diesel (WWE185) replaced the 2.0 D-4D. Production ended in 2018 and the Auris nameplate was retired, replaced by the Corolla.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Toyota Auris?
items.a: The Toyota Auris was offered with five engine families across two generations. The Mk1 (2007–2012) featured 1.4 VVT-i (4ZZ-FE, 2007–2008), 1.33 Dual VVT-i (1NR-FE), 1.6 Dual VVT-i (1ZR-FE), 1.8 Valvematic (2ZR-FAE), 1.4 D-4D (1ND-TV), 2.0 D-4D (1AD-FTV), 2.2 D-4D 180 (2AD-FHV), and 1.8 Hybrid (2ZR-FXE). The Mk2 (2012–2018) added the 1.2 Turbo (8NR-FTS) and 1.6 D-4D (WWE185), with the 1.6 Valvematic and 2.0 D-4D phased out after 2015. All engines are available as used or reconditioned units from Engined.

items.q: How do I identify which engine is in my Auris?
items.a: Check the V5C registration document's engine code field (box D.2), or look for the engine code sticker in the service book or under the bonnet. For Mk1 models, codes include 4ZZ-FE (1.4, 2007–2008), 1NR-FE (1.33), 1ZR-FE (1.6), 2ZR-FAE (1.8), 1ND-TV (1.4 diesel), 1AD-FTV (2.0 diesel), 2AD-FHV (2.2 diesel), and 2ZR-FXE (1.8 Hybrid). For Mk2 models, codes include 1NR-FE (1.33), 1ZR-FAE (1.6, 2012–2015), 8NR-FTS (1.2 Turbo, 2015–2018), 2ZR-FXE (1.8 Hybrid), 1ND-TV (1.4 diesel), 1AD-FTV (2.0 diesel, 2012–2015), and WWE185 (1.6 diesel, 2015–2018). If you're unsure, enter your registration on our site for a confirmed fitment check.

items.q: Used vs reconditioned — which is right for my Auris?
items.a: The Auris Hybrid (2ZR-FXE) shares its engine with the Prius and Lexus CT — a large used market exists. Used engines are cost-effective for older Mk1 models where vehicle value may not justify reconditioning costs. Reconditioned engines offer peace of mind with warranty for Mk2 models still in daily family use. The 1.33 (1NR-FE) and 1.6 (1ZR-FE/FAE) petrols are widely available used across the Toyota range (Yaris, Corolla, Avensis). The 2.2 D-4D (2AD-FHV) is a high-performance diesel; check for DPF and EGR issues at higher mileages.

Each engine is inspected before dispatch, and we provide clear fitment guidance to ensure you get the right engine for your Auris. Buy with confidence knowing your engine is covered and delivered to your door.

items.text: The first-generation Avensis (T220) introduced the 1.6 3ZZ-FE and 1.8 1ZZ-FE VVT-i petrol engines and the 2.0 1CD-FTV D-4D diesel at its 2000 midlife revision, making it the first European Toyota with a D-4D unit.
The second-generation (T250) launched in 2003 with a wider petrol range including the 1AZ-FSE and short-lived 2AZ-FSE, while the diesel line expanded with the 2AD-FTV and 2AD-FHV units.

The third-generation (T270) arrived in 2009 with the Valvematic petrol family (1ZR-FAE, 2ZR-FAE, 3ZR-FAE), and the 2015 facelift introduced BMW-sourced N47-based diesel engines (1WW, 2WW), replacing the Toyota diesel units until production ceased in 2018.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Toyota Avensis?
items.a: The Avensis was offered with four distinct engine families across its production run. Petrol engines included the early 1.6 3ZZ-FE and 1.8 1ZZ-FE VVT-i units (2000–2009), the 2.0 1AZ-FSE and 2.4 2AZ-FSE (2003–2005), and the later Valvematic family: 1.6 1ZR-FAE, 1.8 2ZR-FAE, and 2.0 3ZR-FAE (2009–2018). Diesel engines included the 2.0 D-4D units (1CD-FTV, 1AD-FTV), the 2.2 D-4D 150 (2AD-FTV), the 2.2 D-CAT 180 (2AD-FHV), and from 2015, BMW-sourced N47-based units (1WW and 2WW). This range covers all UK-market petrol and diesel Avensis models.

items.q: How do I identify which engine my Avensis has?
items.a: Check your V5C registration document — the engine code is listed in Section 4 (Vehicle details). For pre-2015 models, common codes include 3ZZ-FE (1.6 petrol), 1ZZ-FE (1.8 petrol), 1AZ-FSE (2.0 petrol), 1CD-FTV (2.0 diesel, 2003–2006), 1AD-FTV (2.0 diesel, 2006–2015), 2AD-FTV (2.2 diesel 150), and 2AD-FHV (2.2 diesel 177). For 2015–2018 models with BMW-sourced diesels, look for 1WW (1.6) or 2WW (2.0). You can also use an online reg-checker service (e.g., the DVLA vehicle enquiry service) for rapid confirmation.

items.q: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Avensis engine?
items.a: This depends on your budget and the age of your vehicle. For newer T270 models (2009–2018), used engines with low mileage are often the most cost-effective option. For the 1AZ-FSE 2.0 petrol, be aware of known oil consumption issues due to piston ring wear — a reconditioned engine with new rings may be a better long-term investment. For high-mileage diesel engines (1CD-FTV, 1AD-FTV, 2AD family), reconditioned units with new injectors, timing components, and turbochargers offer greater reliability than a high-mileage used unit. The BMW-sourced N47 diesels (2015–2018) have known timing chain concerns — a reconditioned unit with updated chain components is recommended for higher-mileage examples.

items.q: What is your warranty and delivery standard?
items.a: All GMC engines come with a standard warranty covering mechanical failure. Delivery is to a UK mainland address of your choice (commercial address preferred; residential delivery may be possible subject to vehicle access). Used engines are photographed and compression-tested before dispatch; reconditioned engines are fully rebuilt with new gaskets, seals, timing components, and bearings. items.text: The first-generation Yaris (XP10, 1999-2005) launched with a 1.0-litre three-cylinder (1KR-FE) and later gained 1.3 (2NZ-FE) and 1.5 (1NZ-FE) petrols, plus a 1.4 D-4D diesel (1ND-TV) from 2002.
The second generation (XP90, 2005-2011) continued the 1.0 (1KR-FE) and 1.3 (2NZ-FE, later 1NR-FE) petrols, joined by a 1.8 (2ZR-FE) in 2007, with the 1.4 D-4D remaining available.

The third generation (XP130, 2011-2020) kept the 1.0 (1KR-FE) and 1.33 (1NR-FE), while the 1.5 Hybrid (1NZ-FXE) debuted in 2012 and the 1.4 D-4D was phased out; a limited-run 1.8 supercharged GRMN appeared in 2017.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Toyota Yaris?
items.a: The Toyota Yaris has used three core engine families across four generations: Valvematic 1.0/1.33 (1KR-FE, 1NR-FE), Hybrid/Valvematic 1.8-2.0 (1NZ-FXE, 2ZR-FE, M15A-FXE, M15A-FKS), and D-4D 1.4 (1ND-TV). Additionally, early 1.3 (2NZ-FE) and GR Yaris 1.6 turbo (G16E-GTS) engines exist but are not yet covered by the BRF. The engine fitted depends on the generation and trim level chosen.

items.q: How do I identify which engine my Yaris has?
items.a: Check the V5C logbook for the engine number — the first characters indicate the engine family (e.g., 1KR, 1NR, 1ND, 2ZR, M15A, G16E). Alternatively, use the registration number with an online parts catalogue or enter your reg on our site for instant fitment verification. For transition years (e.g., 2009), confirming the engine code is essential as two different engines may appear in the same model year.

items.q: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Yaris engine?

For lower-volume or performance engines (2ZR-FE, G16E-GTS), reconditioned units may be the more reliable option. Consider your budget and how long you plan to keep the car when choosing between used and reconditioned.

options.text: For GM-era petrols (Ecotec Family 0, A14NET), used engines are widely available and generally robust. items.text: The Astra H launched with GM's Ecotec Family 0 petrol range (1.4, 1.6, 1.8, 2.0 Turbo) and a diverse diesel lineup including the Fiat-Multijet 1.3 CDTI, the GM-Isuzu 1.6/1.7/2.0 CDTI family, and the Family Z 1.9 CDTI. The 1.9 CDTI (120–150PS) was the volume diesel in the UK used market.
The Astra J introduced the A14NET 1.4 turbo petrol as a core engine, replacing the older Ecotec NA petrols for many buyers.
Diesel offerings continued with the 1.3 CDTI, 1.6/1.7 CDTI, and a 2.0 CDTI (160PS) and 2.0 BiTurbo CDTI (195PS).

The Astra K marked the 2017 Stellantis acquisition split — pre-2018 models used GM-era engines (Ecotec 1.0/1.4/1.6, 1.6 CDTI, 2.0 CDTi B20DTH), while post-2018 models switched to PSA-shared engines: EB2 1.2 PureTech and DV5 1.5 BlueHDi. The Astra L continues with PSA-shared engines: EB2 1.2 PureTech, DV5 1.5 BlueHDi, and a 1.6 PHEV variant.

items.q: What engines are fitted to the Vauxhall Astra?
items.a: The Astra has used 6 engine families across its five generations since 2004. Petrol: Ecotec Family 0 (1.0–2.0, 2004–2019), A14NET (1.4 turbo, 2009–2018), EB2/PureTech (1.2 turbo, 2018–present), and a 1.5 PSA petrol (2023–present). Diesel: 1.3 CDTI (Fiat-Multijet, 2005–2013), 1.5 BlueHDi/DV5 (2018–present), and B20DTH 2.0 CDTi (2015–present). Conditional hubs (1.6/2.0 CDTI, Family Z 1.9 CDTI) are pending escalation to CORE status. Each Astra generation uses a distinct mix of these families — check your chassis code to confirm fitment.

items.q: How do I identify my Astra's engine?
items.a: Use a free online vehicle registration checker (e.g., DVLA vehicle enquiry, Parkers) to confirm the exact engine code. The V5C logbook shows the engine number and capacity. The engine code is stamped on the engine block — for GM-era engines, the code is on the engine plate near the timing cover; for Stellantis-era engines, the code is on the engine type plate. For the 1.9 CDTI, check the engine plate for "Z19" codes; for the 1.3 CDTI, look for "A13" codes. Transition-year Astras (2017–2018) may have either GM-era or Stellantis-era engines — always verify by registration.

items.q: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Astra engine?
items.a: For GM-era petrols (Ecotec Family 0, A14NET), used engines are widely available and generally robust — the 1.4 turbo has a known timing chain stretch issue, making reconditioned units preferable if the chain has not been replaced recently. For the 1.9 CDTI diesel, reconditioned units are recommended due to age-related injector and DPF wear. For post-2018 Stellantis engines (PureTech, BlueHDi), used units are the default — these engines are newer and generally reliable. Reconditioned units offer the best value for older, high-mileage Astra engines with known failure patterns.

items.text: The Insignia launched in 2008 with 1.6 115 PS, 1.8 140 PS, 2.0 Turbo 220 PS, and 2.8 V6 Turbo 260 PS petrols, alongside three 2.0 diesels: 110, 130 and 160 PS. The 2013 facelift brought 1.6 SIDI Turbo 170 PS and 2.0 SIDI Turbo 250 PS petrols, plus revised diesels from 120 to 195 PS. The new-generation 2.0 CDTI 170 PS (B20DTH) arrived in late 2014, with 1.6 CDTI diesels (120/136 PS) following in 2015. The second-generation Insignia launched in 2017 with 1.5 EcoTec Turbo petrols, 1.5 CDTI diesel, and B20DTH continuing from the Mk I. A 2.0 BiTurbo CDTI (210 PS) arrived later. Production ended in 2022.

items.q: What engines are fitted to the Vauxhall Insignia?

A significant number of additional engine families (2.0 Turbo petrol, 2.8 V6, 1.8 petrol, earlier 2.0 CDTI variants) were omitted from the BRF and await escalation. Across the two generations, the Insignia used a broad mix of GM Ecotec, SIDI, and CDTI families, with outputs from 110 PS to 325 PS.

For transition years between Mk I and Mk II, confirming the chassis code (G09 vs Z18) alongside the engine code ensures correct fitment.

items.text: The Vauxhall Mokka launched in the UK in April 2012 as Vauxhall's first entry in the fast-growing B-segment crossover market. Built on the GM Gamma II platform, it shared its engine line-up with the Opel Mokka and Chevrolet Trax. The initial engine range comprised a 1.4i naturally aspirated petrol (100PS — A14XER Ecotec Family 0), a 1.4T turbo petrol (140PS — A14NET), and a 1.7 CDTi diesel (130PS). The 1.7 CDTi was replaced by the 1.6 CDTi 136 in 2013. The Mokka received a comprehensive facelift in 2016 and was rebadged as "Mokka X" for the UK market, with revised exterior styling and upgraded interior technology. The engine line-up carried over the 1.4T and 1.6 CDTi, with the 1.4T gaining a 150PS option. In 2018, the PSA-sourced 1.2 Turbo (130PS) — part of the EB2/PureTech family — was introduced, replacing the 1.4T in some markets as the Vauxhall brand transitioned to Stellantis ownership. Production ended in 2019.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Vauxhall Mokka?

Petrol options included the 1.4i 100 (A14XER, Ecotec Family 0), 1.4T 140/150 (A14NET), and late-life 1.2 Turbo 130 (EB2F/PureTech, PSA-sourced). Diesel options included the 1.7 CDTi 130 (early, Isuzu-sourced) and 1.6 CDTi 110/136 (A16DTR, GM-Isuzu). The engine fitted depends on model year and trim level.

items.q: How can a Mokka owner identify which engine their car has?
items.a: The engine code is printed on the engine plate (visible under the bonnet) and on the V5C registration document in the "Engine number" field. Mokka engine codes include A14XER (1.4i), A14NET (1.4T), A16DTR (1.6 CDTi), and EB2F (1.2 PureTech). For early 1.7 CDTi models, check the V5C or engine bay plate for the specific code. This is especially important for the 2012–2014 pre-facelift models where diesel engines changed mid-generation.

items.q: Used vs reconditioned — which should a Mokka owner choose?
items.a: For Mokka engines, the A14NET turbo petrol and A16DTR diesel are high-volume units with established UK replacement demand. Used engines are a cost-effective option for older Mokkas (2012–2016), while reconditioned units may be preferred for Mokka X models (2016–2019) where lower-mileage used stock is scarcer. The PSA-sourced 1.2 PureTech (2018–2019) is supported through Citroen's existing EB2 hub. items.text: The B5 and B5.5 Passats (1997–2005) established the model’s diesel reputation with the 1.9 TDI PD family (AHU/AFN/AVB/AVF/AWX), while the 1.8 Turbo (AEB) and distinctive 2.3 V5 (AGZ) brought petrol choice; the 2.8 V6 (ACK/ALG) and 2.5 V6 TDI offered six-cylinder refinement.

The B6 (2005–2010) introduced the full VAG modular suite: EA111 2.0 FSI (BLR/BVY), EA189 2.0 TDI (BMP/BKP then CBAB/CBAC), and the first EA888 2.0 TSI (CAWB), with the R36’s 3.6 VR6 (BWS) delivering 300 PS.

The B7 (2010–2014) continued with EA189 diesels (CFFB/CFGC) and EA211 1.4 TSI (CAXA/CTHD) petrols alongside the 1.8 TSI (CDAA). Finally, the MQB-platform B8 (2014–2024) shifted to EA288 diesels (CRLB/CRLD/DBGA/DBGB/CUAA) and EA211 petrols (CZCA/CZDA/CZEA), later adding the 1.5 TSI (DADA/DPCA) and EA888 evo4 2.0 TSI (DKZA/DNNA).
The GTE PHEV (CUKC/DGEB) combined the 1.4 TSI with an electric motor, while the BiTDI (CUAA) offered 240 PS from the 2.0 TDI.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Volkswagen Passat?
items.a: The Passat has used VAG's EA111, EA189, EA211, EA288 and EA888 engine families across its B5–B8 generations, with petrol options ranging from 1.4 TSI to 3.6 VR6 and diesel options from 1.6 TDI to 2.0 BiTDI. The B5/B5.5 era also used the 1.9 TDI PD family and the 2.3 V5.

items.text: The fourth-generation Polo introduced the PQ24 platform, shared with SEAT Ibiza and Škoda Fabia. The 1.4-litre petrol alone carried seven different engine codes across the production window. The May 2005 facelift brought updated engine offerings including the 1.8T GTI.

The fifth-generation Polo introduced TSI and DSG combinations for the first time. The 2014 facelift replaced the 1.2 TSI EA111 with the 1.2 TSI EA211 — a key transition from timing chain to timing belt.

The sixth-generation Polo moved to the MQB A0 platform. Petrol engines are exclusively EA211-family 1.0 MPI and 1.0 TSI three-cylinder units. Diesel offerings continued with 1.6 TDI four-cylinder common-rail across the range.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Volkswagen Polo?

Diesel engines include 1.2 TDI, 1.4 TDI (PD and CR), 1.6 TDI, 1.9 SDI and 1.9 TDI PD. Engine codes vary by year and output — always check the V5C or engine bay sticker.

items.text: The T-Roc launched in the UK in November 2017 on the Volkswagen Group MQB A1 platform, shared with the Golf Mk7. Initial engine offerings were exclusively petrol: 1.0 TSI (110–115 PS), 1.5 TSI EVO (148–150 PS) and 2.0 TSI (187–190 PS). A 2.0 TDI 150 PS diesel joined in December 2017, followed by a 1.6 TDI 115 PS in August 2018. The range-topping T-Roc R arrived in September 2019, powered by a 300 PS 2.0 TSI. A mid-cycle refresh arrived in Spring 2022 with exterior styling and interior tech updates. The engine line-up remained substantively unchanged, with the same petrol and diesel options carried over. The 1.0 TSI, 1.5 TSI EVO, 2.0 TSI and 2.0 TDI continued as the core powertrains, with the T-Roc R retaining its 300 PS 2.0 TSI.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Volkswagen T-Roc?
items.a: The T-Roc was offered with a range of petrol and diesel engines across its 2017–2025 UK production run. Petrol options included 1.0 TSI (110–115 PS), 1.5 TSI EVO (148–150 PS), 2.0 TSI (187–190 PS) and 2.0 TSI (300 PS, T-Roc R only). Diesel options included 1.6 TDI (114 PS) and 2.0 TDI in 115 PS and 150 PS tune. Three distinct families are represented in the T-Roc range.

items.q: How does an owner identify which engine their T-Roc has?
items.a: The engine code is printed on the vehicle's V5C registration document in the engine number field. It can also be found on a sticker in the spare wheel well or on the timing belt cover. For T-Roc models, common codes include CHYA/CHZB (1.0 TSI), DADA/DADB/DXDB (1.5 TSI), CZPB/DNN (2.0 TSI), DNFC (T-Roc R), and DTTC/DTRD (2.0 TDI). If the registration falls near a model-year transition, cross-check the chassis code with the tables above.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Volkswagen Tiguan?
items.a: The Volkswagen Tiguan has been offered with three Volkswagen Group EA-series engine families across its three generations: EA888, EA288, and EA211. Mk1 used EA888 2.0 TSI and EA189/EA288 2.0 TDI diesels plus EA211 1.4 TSI. Mk2 continued with EA888, EA288, and EA211, adding a 1.4 eHybrid PHEV. Mk3 uses EA888 evo4, EA288evo, and EA211evo2.

items.q: How does a Tiguan owner identify which engine their car has?

The engine code can also be found on a sticker in the spare wheel well, inside the service schedule booklet, or on a label on the cambelt cover.

The second-generation Touareg introduced the 3.0 V6 TSI Hybrid and the 4.2 V8 TDI; the 3.0 V6 TDI remained the volume engine, now producing 204–262 PS.
The third-generation Touareg shares the MLB Evo platform with the Audi Q7 and Bentley Bentayga, with engine options including the 3.0 V6 TSI, 3.0 V6 TDI, 4.0 V8 TDI, and the 3.0 V6 eHybrid/R PHEV.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Volkswagen Touareg?
items.a: The Volkswagen Touareg uses a mix of VAG-shared and VW-distinct engines across its generations: VR6 (3.2/3.6 V6 petrol), EA888 (3.0 V6 TSI petrol/hybrid), EA288-family 3.0 V6 TDI diesel, V10 TDI (5.0 diesel), V8 TDI (4.2 and 4.0 diesel), and the W12 (6.0 petrol). The 3.0 V6 TDI is the most common engine in UK-market Touaregs.

items.q: How do I identify which engine is in my Touareg?

Common Touareg codes include BKS, CASA, CRCA (3.0 TDI), AYH/BLE (V10 TDI), AXQ/BAR (4.2 V8), and BHK/CGRA (3.6 VR6). For hybrid models, look for CGFA (Mk2) or BHEV (Mk3).

The 3.6 VR6 and EA888 petrol units sit between the two, with good used availability and reasonable reconditioned costs.

Diesel options transitioned from 1.9 TDI and 2.0 TDI PD (2003–2010) to 1.6 TDI and 2.0 TDI common-rail (2010–2015). The second-generation (Typ 5T, 2015–2022) adopted the MQB platform, using EA211 petrol units (1.2 TSI, 1.4/1.5 TSI, and 1.8 TSI) and EA288 diesel units (1.6 TDI and 2.0 TDI). The Touran was withdrawn from the UK market in 2022/2023.

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Volkswagen Touran?
items.a: The Volkswagen Touran uses 4 confirmed engine families across two generations. Mk1 (2003–2015) includes EA111 petrols (1.6 FSI, 2.0 FSI) and EA189 diesel (2.0 TDI PD). Mk2 (2015–2022) uses EA211 petrols (1.2/1.4/1.5 TSI) and EA288 diesels (1.6/2.0 TDI). Always verify your specific engine code.

items.q: How do I identify which engine my Touran has?
items.a: Check your V5C registration document — the engine number and engine code are listed in the vehicle details section. Alternatively, look for the engine code sticker in the spare wheel well or on the timing belt cover. For Mk1 (2003–2015), common codes include BKC/BXE (1.9 TDI), AZV/BKD (2.0 TDI), and BAG/BLF (1.6 FSI). For Mk2 (2015–2022), look for CYVB (1.2 TSI), CZDA (1.4 TSI), CRVA/DFEB (2.0 TDI), or CRKB/DGDA (1.6 TDI).

items.text: The V60 launched on the P3 platform with a range dominated by the D5 five-cylinder diesel (D5244T family) in 205 PS, along with D3/D4 5-cylinder diesel derivatives (150–177 PS). Petrol options included a 1.6 T4 (B4164T) and later 2.0 T5 (B4204T9/T11) and T6 (B4204T7/T10) Drive-E petrols. The facelift (2013–2015) introduced Drive-E 4-cylinder diesels (D3/D4/D5) as replacements for the 5-cylinder units.

A diesel-electric PHEV (D6) was offered from 2012 using a 2.4-litre 5-cylinder diesel (D5244T20) paired with an electric motor. The second-generation V60 moved to the SPA platform and introduced the B-series mild-hybrid petrols (B3/B4/B5, 2.0-litre, 48V MHEV) and continued with T6/T8 plug-in hybrids (B4204T39, 2.0-litre petrol with supercharger and turbocharger, plus electric motor). Diesel options shifted to mild-hybrid B4/B5 diesels (D420T8/D420T6).

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Volvo V60?
items.a: Volvo V60 engines span four CORE hubs: Legacy D5 2.4 5-cylinder diesel (2001-2014, covers early Gen 1), Drive-E diesel 2.0 4-cylinder (2014-present, covers late Gen 1 and early Gen 2), Drive-E petrol (2014-present, covers T-series petrols and PHEV combustion engines), and B5 mild-hybrid (2019-present, covers B-series MHEV petrol/diesel). A 1.6 T4 petrol (B4164T family) is currently MISSING from the BRF and awaits escalation.

items.q: How do I identify which engine my V60 has?
items.a: Check the V5C registration document for the engine number; the engine code is also stamped on the engine block plate. V60 engine codes include D5244T (various subcodes), D4204T (various), B4204T (various), B420T2, D420T8, D420T6, and B4164T.

items.q: Should I buy a used or reconditioned V60 engine?
items.a: For V60's D5 five-cylinder diesel (Legacy D5), used engines are widely available and cost-effective. For Drive-E diesel and petrol, timing belt and EGR system condition should be checked — reconditioned units may offer better reliability for high-mileage cars. For B5 mild-hybrids, used engines are typically sufficient as these are newer and lower-mileage.

items.q: What warranty and delivery do you offer?
items.a: All GMC engines are supplied with a standard warranty; delivery is to UK mainland addresses. Buyers should confirm engine code matches their vehicle's V5C before purchase.

items.text: The V90 launched in 2016 as the estate sibling to the S90 saloon, built on Volvo's Scalable Product Architecture (SPA).

items.q: What engines were fitted to the Volvo V90?

Petrol: Drive-E four-cylinder (T4/T5/T6, 190–310PS, 2016–2020) and T6/T8 Twin Engine PHEV (340–405PS, 2016–present), followed by B4/B5/B6 petrol MHEV (197–300PS, 2020–present).

items.q: How do I identify my V90's engine?
items.a: Use a free online vehicle registration checker (e.g., DVLA vehicle enquiry, Parkers) to confirm the engine code. The V5C logbook shows the engine number and capacity. The engine code is stamped on the front of the engine block, near the timing cover. For early Drive-E engines, codes begin with "D" (diesel) or "B" (petrol) followed by "4204T" for 2.0-litre four-cylinder turbo. For B-series MHEV, codes begin with "B420T" (petrol) or "D4204T" (diesel).

For Drive-E petrol T4/T5/T6, used units are available; the T6 supercharged+turbo engine is more complex and may benefit from reconditioning. For B-series MHEV engines, used units are the default choice as these engines are newer and generally reliable. For PHEV variants, used units are the only practical choice in the short term.
